extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students in humor studies, cognitive psychology, linguistics, and related humanities/social sciences
extracted.subtask_description: A theoretical account that specifies what psychological state counts as humor and lists conditions and consequences that characterize humor (e.g., incongruity, surprise, aggression, timing, comprehension difficulty). Used to analyze, classify, and predict humorous phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor is affective absurdity
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is a subjective state of apparent emotional absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper's central claim: humor is characterized by an affective (emotional) experience that seems absurd. This is the conceptual core used to explain other properties of humor such as incongruity, surprise, and emotional transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three necessary-and-sufficient conditions for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is fully characterized by three conditions, each separately necessary and jointly sufficient for humor to occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory frames humor formally: all three conditions must be met together for humor to occur; each alone is necessary. (The following rubric entries unpack the three component conditions named in the abstract / headings.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceived situation is seen as normal
rubrics_metrics.description: One condition: the perceived situation must be seen as normal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor requires that, at least initially, the situation is perceived within ordinary expectations or rules; the normalcy of the situation is part of what allows a conflicting appraisal to produce 'absurdity'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective commitment to how something ought to be is violated
rubrics_metrics.description: One condition: some affective commitment of the perceiver to the way something in the situation ought to be is violated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The perceiver must care about (be emotionally committed to) an expectation or 'ought' concerning the situation; humor arises when that commitment is perceived to be breached in a way that produces absurdity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective state of apparent emotional absurdity (joint condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: One condition: the subjective experience must be one of apparent emotional absurdity, arising when normal appearance and violated affective commitment coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This joint condition ties perceived normalcy and violated commitment into the felt experience labeled 'humor'. The paper uses this to explain common humorous effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Violation of the subjective moral order
rubrics_metrics.description: The relevant 'violation' often concerns the perceiver's subjective moral order — their sense of how things ought to be.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper explores what is violated (not just rules or logic but subjective moral expectations). This specifies the domain of the 'ought' implicated in producing humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity (recognized property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity is a recognized property of humor explained by the theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory situates incongruity as a consequence of perceiving normalcy plus a violated affective commitment: two incompatible appraisals produce the sense of absurdity. Incongruity is therefore a diagnostic property of humor instances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surprise (recognized property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Surprise is a characteristic property of many humorous events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise often accompanies the detection of the violated commitment or the incongruity; the paper connects surprise to timing and brevity as factors that enhance humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggression and superiority
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggression (and superiority) are recognized properties that the theory accounts for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper relates aggressive or superiority-based humor to affective commitments being violated in ways that derogate, belittle, or position the perceiver relative to others; such social emotions are explained within the framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional transformation
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often involves emotional transformation — a change in affect triggered by the humorous event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory explains how the shift from one emotional appraisal to another (or to absurdity) is part of humorous experience; this helps account for laughter and other affective responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent comprehension difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Apparent comprehension difficulty is a recognized property of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor can involve moments where comprehension seems difficult or effortful; the paper treats this as part of the process that yields the experience of absurdity and eventual resolution (or not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: brevity and surprise
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing — especially brevity and surprise — is an important factor in producing humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper highlights that concise setup and an unexpected punchline (surprise) amplify the humorous effect; this is presented as a practical rule for producing or evaluating jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehension difficulty as a modulator
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty of comprehension modulates how humor is experienced (e.g., cognitive effort may enhance or reduce humor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper discusses comprehension difficulty alongside timing and surprise; it links cognitive processing demands to degrees of humor and to whether the joke succeeds or fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive restructuring
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor involves cognitive restructuring — a reappraisal of the situation's meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experience of humor often includes a reinterpretation (restructuring) that resolves or reframes the incongruity, producing the affective absurdity described by the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degrees of humor / three-level scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can be graded — the paper posits a three-level scale and consequences for degrees of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than a binary humorous/not-humorous, the theory provides a scale (three levels) to capture varying intensities and kinds of humorous responses; this informs evaluation by magnitude or type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness (role in what is or isn't funny)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniqueness is discussed as relevant to whether something is funny or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper includes a section on 'What isn't funny? Uniqueness' suggesting that lack of uniqueness (predictability, cliché) can reduce humor; uniqueness of the violation or perspective contributes to humorous value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order (sequential/structural considerations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Order — the sequence or organization of elements — affects humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats order as a structural factor (how elements are arranged in time or narrative) that interacts with timing, surprise, and comprehension to produce or impede humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: What isn't funny? (anti-patterns)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper addresses conditions and examples of non-humor — what fails to be funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections on 'What isn't funny?' identify failure modes (e.g., missing affective commitment, lack of perceived normalcy, overexposure, predictable punchlines) that practitioners should avoid; used diagnostically to explain jokes that fall flat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to other theories (competing theoretical views)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor should be evaluated relative to competing accounts such as incongruity, superiority, and Freudian theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper compares its affective-absurdity account to prior theories (absurdity/incongruity, Freud, Raskin) and indicates how different explanatory priorities alter interpretation and classification of humorous material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology / Phenomena of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Various classes and examples of humor phenomena are catalogued: elephant jokes, offensive jokes, peekaboo, giggle-fest, linguistic humor, puns, satire, exaggeration, ridicule, embarrassment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper uses these categories as test cases for the theory — showing how the three conditions and additional factors (timing, comprehension, aggression) explain diverse joke types. This serves as a practical taxonomy for analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic humor (puns and verbal mechanisms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Linguistic mechanisms (wordplay, puns) are treated as specific routes to producing the affective absurdity of humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The theory addresses verbal humor (including Raskin's work) and explains how ambiguity, multiple meanings, or phonological play can instantiate the required conditions for humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offensive jokes and social boundaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Offensive jokes illustrate how violations of social/moral commitments produce humor but also social harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper analyzes offensive material in terms of violated affective commitments and the social/communicational consequences (aggression, superiority), offering guidance for diagnosing misunderstandings and social costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Biological and physiological aspects of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is linked to biological phenomena: physiology of laughter, tickling, crying, gasping in pain, and laughter's bodily correlates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper treats laughter's physiology as part of the empirical consequences of the theory, useful for evaluating or studying humor's bodily manifestations and differentiating laughter types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/communicational functions of humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor has social and communicative roles that the theory explains and that should be considered when evaluating humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sections on social/communicational aspects show how humor manages relationships, signals, and norm enforcement; these functions affect whether humor is appropriate, successful, or harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applications: diagnosing humor-related misunderstandings
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory supplies practical applications such as diagnosing humor-related misunderstandings in everyday life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied guidance includes using the three-condition test to identify why humor failed or was misinterpreted, and steps to mitigate misunderstandings in social interactions.
